pulls.title: Address the comments from adoption.
pulls.author: wkumari
pulls.body:
**Summary:**
Maciej Żenczykowski and others: Changes the requested size to a /48 - this lets containers (e.g ContainerLabs) have multiple /64 networks -- this will require a discussion  with the WG!

Brian Carpenter: Formally update RFC 4007

MCR: Loopback isn't the right term  - add a Node-Local Unicast Prefix term.

Notes: 
Jen kindly summarized the comments received during adoption:

> 1. A concern re: using the 'loopback' term [3],[4]
> 2. The draft should probably update RFC4007 [4]
> 3. The prefix size: multiple comments suggested using /64 [5] 

 See: [https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/ipv6/JDCXJyMXPL_2gl2TjTByVOPNCRc/](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/ipv6/JDCXJyMXPL_2gl2TjTByVOPNCRc/)

Here is longer version, and how I tried to address them:
### Brian Carpenter:
**Comment**: RFC 4007 explicitly states that ::1 does not carry a zone_id.
Maciej: The updated draft lists RFC 4007 in Updates. I added a dedicated section ("Update to RFC 4007") stating that the new prefix belongs to the default node-local loopback zone and MUST NOT be qualified with a zone_id in user interfaces or socket APIs. 

### MCR:
**Comment**: False Loopback Analogy with IPv4: The term "loopback" strictly refers to a single interface looping traffic back to itself. In modern local virtualization (such as container bridges or sidecar proxies), we are dealing with multi-interface node-internal networks.

**Resolution**: Adopted "Node-Local Unicast" Terminology: Added term "Node-Local Unicast Prefix" throughout the document (including Section 1.2 "Terminology and Functional Semantics") to accurately represent the prefix's functional role. I retained the "Loopback" phrasing in the document's title because, well, its the title. I also want people to be able to find this easiler, and "loopback" is a common term.

### Maciej Żenczykowski (and others):
**Comment**: The draft was asking for /96, and this doesn't really work well in practice.

**Resolution**: Wheee, this is a find one. We has started with /32, then something else, then /96, etc. I can't quite remember how we got to /96, but that does really seem like the worst possible number. I'm proposing that we go back to /48 - this allows for having multiple virtual networks (e.g Docker containers, or ContainerLabs) all using normal SLAAC compatible /64s. This was is people want to create things like internal "test" networks within a host they can do so without having to fiddle with things. I really don't think that a /48 is asking for "too much space", but presumably there will be much discussion in the WG on numbers...
